en.title: Surveying and Geoinformatics: the whole course
en.short: What surveying and geoinformatics covers, how the degree is organised, and how to study it.

sections.heading: What surveying and geoinformatics is
sections.text:
Surveying and geoinformatics is the science of measuring, representing and managing information about places on Earth. Surveying covers field measurement of positions, distances, angles and heights, and the computation that turns observations into coordinates, maps and setting-out data. Geoinformatics covers the digital side: geographic information systems (GIS), remote sensing, photogrammetry, spatial databases, geodesy and cartography. Together they support land registration, construction, mapping, transport and environmental management.

The subject matters because spatial data is used to allocate land, design works and manage resources. A small error can cost money or cause a legal dispute.

These summaries teach principles. They do not replace national law, current standards or a registered surveyor. Rules and registration differ by country, so check the current official source.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Programmes differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. In Nigeria, universities commonly offer a BSc in Surveying and Geoinformatics, often four years, while polytechnics offer ND and HND programmes, often two years each, with supervised industrial work. Surveyors are registered by the Surveyors Council of Nigeria (SURCON); the Nigerian Institution of Surveyors is a professional body. COREN registers engineers, not surveyors. In the UK, a bachelor’s degree in surveying or geospatial science is commonly three years, and an integrated master’s four. Professional recognition there usually comes through a body such as RICS.

Early years build mathematics, measurement and mapping. Later years add computation, positioning, geodesy, GIS and professional practice. Most programmes end with a project.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics start with the purpose of the field, then surveying mathematics: trigonometry and coordinate geometry. Measurement errors, accuracy and precision come next, with the physics of optics and electromagnetic measurement. Students then learn linear measurement by chain and tape, angular measurement with compass and theodolite, and levelling with instruments and booking. Maps, scales and contours follow, then survey drawing, CAD and field notes, and finally geospatial data and GIS.

Core topics begin with traversing and coordinate computation. Control surveys cover triangulation, trilateration and networks. Total stations and electromagnetic distance measurement lead to GNSS and satellite positioning. Geodesy, datums and map projections explain the frames behind coordinates. Least-squares adjustment shows how to combine observations and judge their quality. Route surveying covers horizontal and vertical curves, and engineering surveying covers setting out and deformation monitoring. Cadastral surveying and land registration, photogrammetry and UAV mapping, remote sensing, cartography, GIS spatial data models, spatial databases and spatial data infrastructure, hydrographic surveying, and professional practice and ethics complete the core.

At master’s level come advanced geodesy and earth deformation, advanced adjustment and estimation, advanced spatial analysis and geostatistics, and research methods.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Practise the computations by hand until they are routine. Reading a worked example is not the same as producing one. Draw a sketch of every survey before you write an equation, and keep a neat field book: record what you measured, with what instrument, on what date, and who did it. Never rub out a wrong reading; strike it out and write the correction beside it.

Write units on every line, and check that answers are reasonable. Does a traverse close within a few centimetres, or metres? Learn typical magnitudes so you notice mistakes.

Use software after you understand the hand method, and check its output with a simple independent calculation.

keyPoints: Surveying measures and represents the Earth; geoinformatics manages that spatial information digitally.

Degree length, awards and registration differ by country, so check your handbook and the current official body.

en.title: Introduction to Surveying and Geoinformatics
en.short: Definitions, plane versus geodetic surveying, main branches, surveyor roles and professional bodies.

sections.heading: Definitions
sections.text: Surveying is the science and art of measuring and representing positions of points on or near the Earth’s surface, and of setting out those positions on the ground. Geoinformatics is the wider field of acquiring, storing, managing, analysing and displaying geospatial information. Surveying supplies position data; geoinformatics turns it into maps, databases and decisions.

sections.heading: Plane and geodetic
sections.text: Plane surveying treats the Earth as flat. It suits small areas where curvature can be ignored at the accuracy required. Geodetic surveying allows for curvature and suits large areas, long lines and precise national networks. The boundary depends on area, accuracy and instruments, so no single size applies everywhere. Over long distances, a flat-Earth assumption causes errors that grow with distance; over a small plot, plane methods are normal.

sections.heading: Main branches
sections.text: Cadastral surveying defines land parcels for ownership, registration and taxation. Engineering surveying sets out and checks buildings, roads and dams, and monitors movement. Topographic surveying maps natural and built features and ground shape. Hydrographic surveying maps water bodies, seabeds and navigation channels. Control surveying establishes fixed points with known coordinates that support other surveys. The branches overlap: a road may need control, topographic, cadastral and engineering work.

sections.heading: Role and bodies
sections.text: Surveyors serve land, construction and mapping. In land, they fix boundaries and prepare records for title. In construction, they set out positions and check them. In mapping, they provide accurate base data for maps, GIS and planning. Registration differs by country. In Nigeria, the Surveyors Council of Nigeria (SURCON) regulates registration and the Nigerian Institution of Surveyors (NIS) is the professional body. In the United Kingdom, the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors (RICS) is a professional body. In Kenya, the Institution of Surveyors of Kenya (ISK) is a professional body. Check current national law before practising. A made-up case: Amina in Kano, Nigeria, surveys a plot boundary, sets out a school block and supplies map coordinates.

keyPoints: Surveying measures and represents positions and sets out points on the ground.
Geoinformatics manages and analyses geospatial information, including maps and databases.
Plane surveying assumes a flat Earth for small areas; geodetic surveying allows for curvature over large areas.
Cadastral, engineering, topographic, hydrographic and control surveying are main branches.
Surveyors support land title, construction setting out and mapping.
Professional registration differs by country; in Nigeria SURCON regulates and NIS is the professional body.

en.title: Surveying Mathematics: Trigonometry and Coordinate Geometry
en.short: Sine and cosine rules, bearings, coordinate differences, area by coordinates and simple volumes.

sections.heading: Angles and bearings
sections.text:
A bearing is measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°. In a triangle, side a is opposite angle A. The sine rule is a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C. The cosine rule is c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.

Example: AB = 80.000 m, A = 40°, B = 60°, so C = 80°. BC = 80.000 × sin 40° ÷ sin 80° = 52.216 m. Keep metres to three decimals only when the field data justify it.

sections.heading: Coordinates and bearings
sections.text:
Survey coordinates are easting E and northing N in metres. For distance d and bearing θ, ΔE = d sin θ and ΔN = d cos θ. Conversely, d = √(ΔE² + ΔN²) and tan θ = ΔE ÷ ΔN; choose the quadrant from the signs.

Example: A(500.000 E, 1000.000 N) to B(650.000 E, 1120.000 N). ΔE = 150.000 m, ΔN = 120.000 m. d = √(150.000² + 120.000²) = 192.094 m. θ = arctan(150.000 ÷ 120.000) = 51.340°, or 51°20′25″. Reverse bearing = 231.340°.

sections.heading: Area by coordinates
sections.text: Area by coordinates uses the shoelace formula: 2A = Σ(E_i N_{i+1} − E_{i+1} N_i), with points in order and the absolute value taken. For A(500,1000), B(650,1120), C(600,1200), the sum is 1,940,000 − 1,922,000 = 18,000, so A = 9,000 m². Reversing the order changes only the sign.

sections.heading: Volumes and checks
sections.text: Simple volumes: for a prism, V = area × length. For average end areas, V = L(A₁ + A₂) ÷ 2. Example: a trench 40.00 m long with constant cross-section 1.25 m² has V = 1.25 × 40.00 = 50.00 m³. If A₁ = 1.20 m², A₂ = 1.80 m² and L = 20.00 m, V = 20.00 × (1.20 + 1.80) ÷ 2 = 30.00 m³. Check units, significant figures and closure.

keyPoints: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°.
Sine rule: a ÷ sin A = b ÷ sin B = c ÷ sin C; cosine rule: c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C.
With bearing θ from north, ΔE = d sin θ and ΔN = d cos θ; distance d = √(ΔE² + ΔN²).
Bearing θ = arctan(ΔE ÷ ΔN), adjusted to the correct quadrant and expressed from 0° to 360°.
Area by coordinates: 2A = Σ(E_i N_{i+1} − E_{i+1} N_i), taking the absolute value.
Prism volume V = area × length; average end area V = L(A₁ + A₂) ÷ 2; check units and closure.

en.title: Measurement Errors, Accuracy and Precision
en.short: Accuracy, precision, systematic and random errors, mistakes, error propagation and field checks.

sections.heading: Accuracy and precision
sections.text:
Accuracy is how close a result is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated results are to one another. A set can be precise but inaccurate if the same wrong value is repeated.

In surveying, accuracy is usually stated as a limit or a standard deviation; check the current national or project specification, because limits differ by country and purpose.

sections.heading: Error types
sections.text:
A systematic error affects every observation in the same way, for example a tape that is too long or a level with a collimation error. It can often be found and corrected by calibration.

A random error varies in size and sign and cannot be predicted; averaging reduces its effect. A mistake or blunder is a human slip, such as a wrong booking or a misread scale. It is not a random error and must be found and removed, not averaged away.

sections.heading: Propagation and spread
sections.text:
For a sum or difference, independent random errors combine as σ_total = √(σ₁² + σ₂²). For a product or quotient, use relative errors: (σ_z ÷ z)² = (σ_x ÷ x)² + (σ_y ÷ y)². For n repeated observations, the sample standard deviation is s = √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)], and the standard deviation of the mean is s ÷ √n.

Example: four distances 100.02, 100.00, 100.04, 99.98 m. Mean = 100.01 m; deviations are +0.01, −0.01, +0.03, −0.03; Σd² = 0.0020 m²; s = √(0.0020 ÷ 3) = 0.026 m.

sections.heading: Checks and values
sections.text:
The true value is the unknown quantity we want. The observed value is what we measured. The adjusted value is the value after corrections and adjustment.

Field checks reveal blunders: repeat a measurement on a different line or with a different instrument, close a levelling run between known points, check that a triangle’s angles sum to 180° (allowing for spherical excess in large surveys), and compare independent methods. Record checks in the field book.

keyPoints: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results to one another.
Systematic errors repeat in size and sign and are corrected by calibration or procedure; random errors vary and are reduced by averaging.
Mistakes or blunders are human slips and must be found and removed, not averaged.
For independent random errors in a sum or difference, σ_total = √(σ₁² + σ₂²); for products or quotients use relative errors.
For n repeated observations, s = √[Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1)] and the standard deviation of the mean is s ÷ √n.
True value is unknown, observed value is measured, adjusted value is corrected and estimated; field checks such as repeats and closures reveal blunders.

en.title: Physics of Surveying Instruments: Optics and Electromagnetic Measurement
en.short: How telescope optics, refraction and electromagnetic waves let surveyors measure angles and distances.

sections.heading: Telescope optics
sections.text: A surveying telescope gathers light from a target and forms a sharp image. The objective lens has a long focal length. The eyepiece, a short-focus lens, magnifies that image. A reticle (crosshair) sits at the focal plane for aiming. Focusing moves the eyepiece or an internal lens until image and crosshair are both sharp. A level is a telescope fixed to a horizontal line of sight, checked by a spirit bubble or compensator. Prisms fold the light path, erect the image and shorten it.

sections.heading: Reflection and refraction
sections.text: Light travels in straight lines in a uniform medium. Reflection follows a simple rule: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection. At a boundary between media light refracts, or bends, because its speed changes. Snell’s law is n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, where n is the refractive index, the ratio of light’s speed in vacuum to its speed in the medium. A convex lens converges light; a concave lens diverges it. Focal length is the distance from the lens to the point where parallel rays meet. Air temperature and pressure change n, so the line of sight bends and distant objects appear displaced. Surveyors allow for refraction and Earth curvature.

sections.heading: Electromagnetic spectrum
sections.text: Visible light is one small band of the electromagnetic spectrum. The spectrum also includes radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. All travel at about c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum, a little slower in air. Radio and microwave bands suit surveying: they pass through weather and carry coded signals, though many distance meters use infrared or laser light.

sections.heading: Measuring distance
sections.text: An electronic distance meter (EDM) sends a wave to a reflector and measures travel time or phase. For a pulse, distance = c × t ÷ 2 for the out-and-back path. Example: t = 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ s gives d = 3.00 × 10⁸ × 2.00 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 2 = 300 m. Phase methods compare sent and returned waves using wavelength. Satellite ranging times radio signals. Air temperature, pressure and humidity change wave speed, so instruments apply atmospheric corrections.

keyPoints: A telescope objective forms the image and the eyepiece magnifies it; the reticle marks the line of sight.
Reflection: angle of incidence equals angle of reflection; refraction obeys Snell’s law n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r.
A convex lens converges light and has a focal length; prisms use reflection to fold and erect the image.
Visible light is part of the electromagnetic spectrum; all electromagnetic waves travel at about c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
Pulse distance = c × t ÷ 2 for a wave that travels to a target and back.
Atmospheric temperature, pressure and humidity bend light and change radio wave speed, so observations need corrections.

en.title: Linear Measurement: Chain and Tape Surveying
en.short: Chain and tape measurement, ranging, slope corrections, booking and taping errors.

sections.heading: Chain and tape
sections.text: Chain and tape surveying measures distances on the ground. A chain is a linked metal measure; the Gunter chain is 66 ft (20.1168 m) with 100 links. A steel tape is more accurate. Ranging places intermediate points on the straight line between stations, by eye, with a line ranger or with a theodolite. The line is then chained in sections and booked.

sections.heading: Ranging and slopes
sections.text: On sloping ground, measure along the slope and reduce to horizontal. If slope length is L and angle to horizontal is θ, horizontal = L cos θ. Slope correction = L − L cos θ, subtracted from the slope length. For small height difference h, horizontal ≈ L − h² ÷ (2L). Step chaining holds the tape horizontal in short steps with plumb bobs.

sections.heading: Corrections
sections.text:
Corrections: temperature Ct = αL(Tm − Ts), where Tm is the temperature at measurement and Ts the standard temperature; α is about 0.0000112 per °C for steel. Tension Cp = (P − P0)L ÷ (AE), where P is the pull applied, P0 the standard pull, A the cross-section area and E ≈ 200,000 N/mm² for steel. Sag Cs = −w²L³ ÷ (24P²), for span L, weight per length w and tension P. Standard length: if nominal tape l is actually l′, correction = (L ÷ l)(l′ − l).

Example: L = 30.000 m at θ = 5°. Horizontal = 30.000 cos 5° = 29.886 m, so slope correction = −0.114 m. A rise of 10 °C gives Ct = 0.0000112 × 30 × 10 = 0.0034 m.

sections.heading: Booking and errors
sections.text: Booking records station, chainage, measured length, slope, temperature, tension and remarks. Check by measuring forward and back, closing to a known point, or comparing with an optical or electronic distance measurement; allowed difference depends on the specification and country. Main taping errors: non-standard tape, wrong temperature or tension, sag, uncorrected slope, misalignment, reading error, wind, uneven ground and careless booking.

keyPoints: Ranging sets intermediate points on the straight line between two stations before chaining.
On a slope, horizontal distance = L cos θ and the slope correction is L − L cos θ, subtracted from the slope length.
Temperature correction is Ct = αL(Tm − Ts); for steel α is about 0.0000112 per °C.
Tension correction is Cp = (P − P0)L ÷ (AE); sag correction is Cs = −w²L³ ÷ (24P²).
Standard length correction is (L ÷ l)(l′ − l) when nominal tape length l differs from actual l′.
Check linear work by forward and back measurement or closure, and correct for tape standard, temperature, tension, sag and slope.

en.title: Angular Measurement: Compass and Theodolite
en.short: Bearings, true and magnetic north, declination, and measuring angles with compass and theodolite.

sections.heading: Bearings and north
sections.text: A bearing is a direction measured clockwise from a north reference, usually 0° to 360°. True north is geographic north; magnetic north is where a magnetic needle points. The angle between them is magnetic declination. Declination varies with place and time, so use the current value and state its sign. If declination is 5° west, true bearing = magnetic bearing − 5°. Example: magnetic bearing 120° gives true bearing 115°.

sections.heading: Compass and theodolite
sections.text: A magnetic compass gives magnetic bearings directly. A prismatic compass is held level and sighted on the target; iron nearby causes local attraction. A theodolite measures horizontal and vertical angles precisely. Set it up by centring over the station, levelling with the plate levels and footscrews, then focusing the telescope. Horizontal angles lie in the horizontal plane; vertical angles are measured from the horizontal or from the zenith.

sections.heading: Faces and angles
sections.text: Observe on both faces: face left and face right (vertical circle left or right of the telescope). For a direction, the two readings should differ by 180°. The mean removes collimation error and some axis errors. Example: face left 72°14'20'', face right 252°14'40''. Reduce face right by 180° to 72°14'40''; mean = (72°14'20'' + 72°14'40'') ÷ 2 = 72°14'30''. A horizontal angle is the difference between two such directions.

sections.heading: Errors and checks
sections.text: Main instrumental errors are collimation error, horizontal axis not perpendicular to vertical axis, and graduation error. Personal errors include parallax, poor pointing, misreading and mis-centring. Magnetic errors include local attraction and wrong declination. Take face-left and face-right readings, close angles, and repeat observations to control them.

keyPoints: A bearing is measured clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°.
True bearing = magnetic bearing + east declination, or − west declination.
A compass reads magnetic bearings; a theodolite measures horizontal and vertical angles.
Set up a theodolite by centring, levelling and focusing.
Face-left and face-right readings should differ by 180°; their mean reduces instrumental error.
Horizontal angle = difference of two directions; vertical angle is from horizontal or zenith.

en.title: Levelling: Principles, Instruments and Booking
en.short: Datum, reduced level, instruments, booking methods, levelling types, two-peg test and errors.

sections.heading: Datum and instruments
sections.text:
Levelling finds heights relative to a datum, a reference surface. A reduced level (RL) is a height above or below the datum. A bench mark (BM) is a permanent point of known RL; a temporary BM serves one job.

The level on a tripod gives a horizontal line of sight, the line of collimation. A levelling staff is the graduated rod read through the telescope. HI, height of instrument, is the RL of that line.

sections.heading: Booking methods
sections.text:
Height of collimation: HI = RL + backsight; then RL = HI − staff reading. Rise and fall: compare consecutive readings; a smaller reading ahead is a rise, a larger one a fall.

Example: BM A RL 100.000 m. Backsight 1.450 gives HI 101.450. Intermediate sight 1.820 at B gives RL 99.630. Foresight 2.105 at C gives RL 99.345. Rise and fall: 1.450 − 1.820 = −0.370 fall, so 99.630; 1.820 − 2.105 = −0.285 fall, so 99.345. Both agree.

sections.heading: Types of levelling
sections.text:
Differential levelling finds the height difference between two points. Fly levelling is a fast run between bench marks; it must close within an allowed misclosure. Reciprocal levelling uses two setups, near each end of a long sight, averaging results to cancel curvature, refraction and collimation error. Profile levelling reads along a line to plot a section.

Two-peg test checks collimation. Set two pegs apart. With the level midway, read both staffs; the difference is the true difference. Move the level near one peg and read again. A changed difference means the sight is not horizontal.

sections.heading: Checks and errors
sections.text:
Arithmetic check: Σ backsights − Σ foresights = last RL − first RL. Rise-and-fall check: Σ rises − Σ falls = last RL − first RL. Closing error on a fly run is final RL minus known RL; permissible limits vary, so check the local specification.

Errors include instrument maladjustment, staff not vertical, parallax, reading and booking mistakes, tripod settlement, curvature and refraction. Keep sights short and balanced.

keyPoints: RL = HI − staff reading; HI = RL + backsight.
Rise or fall = previous staff reading − next staff reading; a negative result is a fall.
Arithmetic check: Σ backsights − Σ foresights = last RL − first RL.
Rise-and-fall check: Σ rises − Σ falls = last RL − first RL.
The two-peg test detects collimation error by comparing height differences from two instrument positions.
Fly levelling must close on a known bench mark within the misclosure allowed by the local specification.

en.title: Maps, Scales and Contours
en.short: Map scale, representative fractions, symbols, grid references, bearings, contours, relief, areas and sections.

sections.heading: Scale and symbols
sections.text:
Map scale is the ratio of a map distance to the same distance on the ground. It may be a statement (1 cm to 500 m), a representative fraction (RF) such as 1:50,000, or a scale bar. The RF has no units: 1:50,000 means one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground. A plan is a large-scale drawing of a small area; a map covers more ground with more generalisation. Symbols are explained in the legend.

Example: at 1:50,000, 4.2 cm on the map represents 4.2 × 50,000 = 210,000 cm = 2,100 m = 2.1 km.

sections.heading: Grid references and bearings
sections.text: Grid lines are numbered as eastings and northings. Give the easting first, then the northing. A four-figure reference names a grid square; a six-figure reference estimates tenths within it. Grid square size depends on the map, so check the legend. A bearing is an angle measured clockwise from north. To measure one, draw a line from start to target, place a protractor at the start, and read clockwise from a north line through that point.

sections.heading: Contours and relief
sections.text: A contour is a line joining points of equal height above a datum, such as mean sea level. The contour interval is the vertical distance between neighbouring contours. Contours close together show a steep slope; widely spaced contours show a gentle slope. A contour crossing a valley forms a V pointing upstream, towards higher ground. Spot heights give elevations. Relief is the shape and height of the land, read from contours, spot heights and symbols.

sections.heading: Plans, sections and area
sections.text:
To draw a plan, choose a scale that fits the paper, plot the measured points, and add a north arrow and scale. For a section, plot distance along a line against elevation; a larger vertical scale exaggerates relief. Map area scales by the square of the RF.

Example: a map area of 6 cm² at 1:25,000 gives 6 × 25,000² = 3,750,000,000 cm² = 375,000 m² = 0.375 km².

keyPoints: Map scale compares map distance with ground distance; RF = map distance ÷ ground distance in the same units.
Ground distance = map distance × scale denominator, where 1:50,000 has denominator 50,000.
Ground area = map area × (scale denominator)².
Grid references give eastings before northings, and bearings are measured clockwise from north.
Contour interval is the vertical difference between neighbouring contours; close contours mean steep ground.
A plan must state its scale and show a north arrow; a section must state its horizontal and vertical scales and its vertical exaggeration.

en.title: Survey Drawing, CAD and Field Notes
en.short: Field notes, sketches, hand plotting, CAD layers, coordinates, linework, annotation and checks.

sections.heading: Field notes and sketches
sections.text: Field notes are the record made at the instrument: date, observer, instrument, readings, sketch and remarks. Write in ink or a hard pencil (practice varies) and never erase; cross out a wrong figure once and write the correction beside it. A survey sketch is a freehand plan of stations, features, north and reference marks. It need not be to scale, but say so. Survey records include booking sheets, logs, photographs and digital files. Keep them together and back them up.

sections.heading: Plotting the data
sections.text: Plotting turns field observations into a drawing. By hand, you set a scale, draw the grid and reference lines, then plot each station from its coordinates or by intersection of rays from two known points, using a sharp pencil and a scale rule. With computer-aided drafting (CAD), you type coordinates and the software draws the linework. In modern practice both routes usually start the same way: reduce the observations to coordinates before plotting.

sections.heading: Layers and coordinates
sections.text: A layer is a named level in a CAD file that holds one kind of content, such as boundaries, contours or text. Layers let you switch parts on and off, colour them and lock them against accidental editing. Coordinates are the numbers that fix each point, usually easting (x) and northing (y) on a stated grid. Linework joins those points: straight lines between stations, smooth curves for features. Snap tools keep ends exactly on points.

sections.heading: Annotation and checking
sections.text: Annotation is the text and symbols that make a drawing readable: point numbers, coordinates, heights, scale bar, north arrow, legend, title and date. Check the drawing against the field observations before issuing it. Pick a few stations and compare the plotted coordinates with the booking sheet; measure a known distance on the plot and convert it with the scale. Example: two stations 50.00 m apart on the ground, plotted at 1:500, must be 100 mm apart on paper (50.00 m ÷ 500 = 0.100 m).

keyPoints: Field notes are written at the instrument and never erased; a wrong figure is crossed out once and the correction written beside it.
Reduce observations to coordinates before plotting; this is the usual first step, by hand or in CAD.
A layer holds one kind of content and can be switched on or off, coloured or locked.
Coordinates are usually easting (x) and northing (y) on a stated grid.
Annotate every drawing with scale, north arrow, legend, title and date.
Check the plot against the booking sheet: at 1:500, 50.00 m on the ground is 100 mm on paper.

en.title: Geospatial Data and GIS: An Introduction
en.short: Geospatial data, raster and vector models, layers, attributes, coordinate systems and basic GIS queries.

sections.heading: Geospatial data
sections.text: Geospatial data describes things by where they are. Each feature usually has geometry (a point, line or area) and attributes, which are facts stored in a table, such as a parcel number or land use. Data are organised in layers: one layer for roads, another for buildings. A layer holds features of one kind, and layers can be drawn together because they share a coordinate system.

sections.heading: Raster and vector
sections.text: Two models store geometry. The vector model uses points, lines and polygons with exact coordinates; it suits parcels, pipes and boundaries. The raster model divides space into a grid of cells, each holding a value such as elevation or land cover; it suits continuous surfaces and satellite images. Vector files stay sharp when enlarged, while raster detail depends on cell size.

sections.heading: Coordinates and GIS parts
sections.text: A coordinate reference system (CRS) is the rule that ties coordinates to the Earth. Geographic coordinates use latitude and longitude; projected coordinates use metres on a flat map, such as Universal Transverse Mercator (UTM). A GIS has hardware, software, data, people and methods. People and methods matter: a GIS is not only software.

sections.heading: Queries, overlays, differences
sections.text: A query selects features by attribute or location. In a made-up case, a planner has a parcels layer and a flood-zone layer. The attribute query area > 500 m² might return 12 parcels; the spatial overlay of parcels with the flood zone returns the parcels inside it, say 3. Overlay combines layers to create new information. GIS differs from computer-aided drafting (CAD): CAD draws precise designs but has limited attribute tables and analysis. GIS also differs from surveying measurement: surveying observes positions in the field, while GIS stores, links and analyses those positions with other data.

keyPoints: Geospatial data links location, stored as geometry, to attributes.
Vector uses points, lines and polygons; raster uses grid cells.
Layers group similar features and share a coordinate reference system.
A GIS has hardware, software, data, people and methods.
Attribute queries select by table values; overlays combine layers by location.
GIS analyses mapped data, CAD drafts designs, and surveying measures positions in the field.

en.title: Traversing and Coordinate Computation
en.short: Open and closed traverses, bearings, latitudes and departures, misclosure adjustment and area from coordinates.

sections.heading: Traverse types
sections.text: A traverse is a series of connected lines whose lengths and directions are measured. A closed traverse returns to its start or to a known point, so it can be checked. An open traverse ends without closure; check it by repeating readings and tying to known control. Bearings are whole-circle angles clockwise from north. Angles may be interior angles; for a closed polygon of n sides their sum should be (n − 2) × 180°.

sections.heading: Latitudes and departures
sections.text: For a line of length d and bearing θ, latitude ΔN = d cos θ and departure ΔE = d sin θ. North and east are positive; south and west negative. In a closed traverse ΣΔN and ΣΔE should be zero. Their residuals are the misclosure. Linear misclosure = √((ΣΔE)² + (ΣΔN)²). Precision is misclosure ÷ perimeter, often written 1 in P/m.

sections.heading: Adjustment
sections.text: Bowditch (compass) rule spreads the misclosure in proportion to line length: correction to ΔE = −ΣΔE × (d ÷ perimeter), and similarly for ΔN. The transit rule uses the size of each latitude or departure instead of length. Bowditch suits random errors in angles and distances of similar size; transit suits when the angular measurements are more precise than the linear ones. Apply corrections with signs opposite the misclosure.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: Triangle A(0,0), B(100,0), C(0,100), with coordinates as eastings and northings. Measured: AB 90°, 100.000 m; BC 315°, 141.421 m; CA 180°, 99.000 m. ΔN: 0, +100.000, −99.000; sum +1.000. ΔE: +100.000, −100.000, 0; sum 0. Perimeter 340.421 m. Bowditch corrections to ΔN: AB −0.294, BC −0.415, CA −0.291. Adjusted coordinates: B(100.000, −0.294), C(0.000, 99.291). Area = ½|Σ(x_i y_{i+1} − y_i x_{i+1})| = ½(100 × 99.291) = 4,964.55 m².

keyPoints: A closed traverse returns to a known point and can be checked by angular and linear closure; an open traverse needs repeated readings and ties to control.
For a line of length d and bearing θ, latitude ΔN = d cos θ and departure ΔE = d sin θ, with north and east positive.
In a closed traverse, ΣΔN = 0 and ΣΔE = 0; linear misclosure = √((ΣΔE)² + (ΣΔN)²).
Angular misclosure for an n-sided polygon = sum of measured interior angles − (n − 2) × 180°.
Bowditch correction to a coordinate difference = −misclosure × (line length ÷ perimeter).
Area from coordinates = ½|Σ(x_i y_{i+1} − y_i x_{i+1})|.

en.title: Control Surveys: Triangulation, Trilateration and Networks
en.short: Horizontal and vertical control, triangulation, trilateration, intersection, resection, baselines and accuracy.

sections.heading: Control networks
sections.text: A control survey establishes points whose coordinates or elevations are known to high accuracy. Horizontal control gives eastings and northings; vertical control gives elevations, often at benchmarks, which are permanent marks of known height. Detail surveys, engineering setting out and cadastral (land boundary) surveys are tied to these points, so small control errors do not grow across a site. Control may be national, regional or local; each country runs its own network through a named agency, so check the official source.

sections.heading: Triangulation and trilateration
sections.text: Triangulation measures the angles of a chain or network of triangles plus at least one baseline, a distance measured with great care. The sine rule then gives the other sides. Trilateration measures the sides and computes the angles. Modern work uses electromagnetic distance measurement (EDM) or GNSS for distances. Example: baseline AB = 1000.000 m, angle A = 60°, angle B = 50°, so angle C = 70°. Then AC = AB × sin 50° ÷ sin 70° = 1000 × 0.76604 ÷ 0.93969 = 815.21 m.

sections.heading: Intersection, resection, design
sections.text: Intersection fixes a new point by observing it from two or more known points. Resection fixes the instrument station itself by observing known points; the three-point resection is common, and the station lies on a danger circle if the three known points and the station are concyclic, which weakens the fix. Network design chooses the shape, the number of redundant observations and instrument precision so the required accuracy is reached at reasonable cost. Well-shaped triangles and checks on every figure matter.

sections.heading: Accuracy and adjustment
sections.text: Accuracy is judged by misclosure: the difference between computed and known values, such as the sum of triangle angles against 180° plus spherical excess. Tolerances differ by country and project specification, so quote the project or national specification rather than a remembered number. Observations are usually adjusted, for example by least squares, so corrections are spread consistently.

keyPoints: Control points are the accurate framework to which detail, engineering and cadastral surveys are tied.
Triangulation measures angles from a measured baseline; trilateration measures the sides.
Sine rule: side AC = AB × sin B ÷ sin C.
Intersection fixes an unknown point; resection fixes the instrument station.
Three-point resection is weak when the station lies on the danger circle.
Misclosure against known values is the basic test of control accuracy; tolerances vary by country and project.

en.title: Total Stations and Electromagnetic Distance Measurement
en.short: EDM, total station functions, prism constants, atmospheric corrections, field procedures, data transfer and checks.

sections.heading: EDM principle
sections.text: Electromagnetic distance measurement (EDM) sends a modulated light or microwave signal to a reflector and back. The instrument compares the phase of the outgoing and returning modulation. The known modulation wavelength gives the fractional distance; several frequencies resolve the whole-number ambiguity. The result is a slope distance. The speed of light in air varies with temperature, pressure and humidity, so an atmospheric correction is applied.

sections.heading: Total station functions
sections.text: A total station combines an electronic theodolite, an EDM and a computer with memory. It measures horizontal and vertical angles and slope distance, then computes horizontal distance and height difference. It can set out points, record point codes and heights, and transfer data to software. Angles are read from electronic circles.

sections.heading: Prism and atmosphere
sections.text: The prism constant is a small offset between the prism’s optical centre and the point being measured. It depends on the prism and must match the instrument setting; a wrong value shifts every distance. Atmospheric correction uses temperature, pressure and humidity to adjust for the actual speed of light. Enter field values or use the instrument’s sensors. Manufacturer manuals give the correct sign and method, which differ between instruments.

sections.heading: Fieldwork and checks
sections.text:
Set up over the station mark, centre and level the instrument, and measure its height. Set the prism height at the target. Take a backsight to a known point, then observe angles and distances, preferably angles on both faces. Record point number, code, height and remarks, then transfer the file by cable, USB or Bluetooth and check it in the office.

Example: slope distance S = 100.000 m and zenith angle z = 60° (measured from the vertical) give H = S sin z = 100.000 × sin 60° = 86.603 m, and V = S cos z = 50.000 m.

Check against known control, repeat readings, and confirm prism constant and atmospheric settings. Limitations include line-of-sight obstruction, limited range, heat shimmer, wrong heights or centring, and battery or memory failure.

keyPoints: EDM measures slope distance by comparing the phase of a modulated signal returned from a prism.
A total station combines electronic angle measurement, EDM, computing and data storage.
Prism constant must match the prism and instrument setting; atmospheric correction uses temperature, pressure and humidity.
Horizontal distance H = S sin z and height difference V = S cos z for slope distance S and zenith angle z.
Field checks include centring, instrument and prism heights, backsight, repeated readings, and known control.
Limitations include line-of-sight obstruction, range, heat shimmer, setting errors and power or memory failure.

en.title: GNSS and Satellite Positioning
en.short: GNSS constellations, signals, pseudorange and phase, static, kinematic and RTK, coordinates and errors.

sections.heading: Constellations and signals
sections.text: GNSS means Global Navigation Satellite System. The global constellations are GPS (United States), GLONASS (Russia), Galileo (European Union) and BeiDou (China); QZSS (Japan) and NavIC (India) are regional. Satellites broadcast L-band carrier waves that carry ranging codes and a navigation message. A receiver times a code to get a pseudorange, a range spoiled by clock errors. It also measures carrier phase, which is very precise but ambiguous: the whole number of cycles between satellite and antenna is unknown.

sections.heading: Observation methods
sections.text: Pseudorange gives metre-level positions. Carrier phase gives millimetre to centimetre precision once the integer ambiguity is resolved. In static surveying, a receiver stays on a point for minutes to hours and baselines are processed later. Kinematic surveying tracks a moving receiver. RTK (real-time kinematic) sends corrections from a base station or network to a rover by radio or internet, giving centimetre positions in real time. Precise methods need two receivers or precise satellite products.

sections.heading: Coordinates and errors
sections.text: GNSS computes positions in an Earth-centred, Earth-fixed (ECEF) Cartesian frame. Surveyors convert these to latitude, longitude and ellipsoidal height, then apply a datum transformation, often a seven-parameter Helmert transformation, and a map projection to get local grid coordinates. Errors come from satellite clocks and orbits, the ionosphere and troposphere, multipath (reflected signals), receiver noise and poor satellite geometry, measured by DOP (dilution of precision).

sections.heading: Accuracy and limits
sections.text: Under good conditions, pseudorange is metre-level, while RTK and static carrier phase are centimetre-level or better. Example: the GPS L1 carrier frequency is 1575.42 MHz. Wavelength = speed of light ÷ frequency = 299,792,458 ÷ 1,575,420,000 = 0.1903 m, about 19 cm. A phase measurement good to 0.01 cycle is therefore about 1.9 mm in range. GNSS needs a clear view of the sky. It is weak under dense canopy, in tunnels and in urban canyons, and ellipsoidal heights need a geoid model for orthometric heights. Check local standards for accuracy.

keyPoints: GNSS constellations include GPS, GLONASS, Galileo and BeiDou, with QZSS and NavIC regional.
Pseudorange is code-based and metre-level; carrier phase is precise but has an integer ambiguity.
Static, kinematic and RTK differ in whether the receiver stays still, moves, or gets real-time corrections.
GNSS positions are ECEF; local grid coordinates need datum transformation and map projection.
Main errors are clocks, orbits, atmosphere, multipath, receiver noise and poor satellite geometry (high DOP).
Carrier wavelength = c ÷ f; for GPS L1, 0.01 cycle is about 1.9 mm.

en.title: Geodesy, Datums and Map Projections
en.short: Earth shape, geoid, ellipsoid, datums, coordinates, UTM and datum transformations.

sections.heading: Earth shape and geoid
sections.text: Earth is nearly spherical but flattened at the poles and irregular. The geoid is the equipotential surface of gravity that best approximates mean sea level. It undulates because mass is unevenly distributed. A reference ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical surface fitted to the Earth. The separation between geoid and ellipsoid is the geoid undulation. Surveying needs the ellipsoid for coordinates and the geoid for heights.

sections.heading: Datums and coordinates
sections.text: A horizontal datum fixes an ellipsoid, its origin and its orientation so that latitude and longitude are defined. A vertical datum fixes the zero for heights, often mean sea level at a named tide gauge. Common coordinates are geographic latitude, longitude and ellipsoidal height; geocentric Cartesian X, Y, Z; and projected easting and northing. Height above the geoid is orthometric height; height above the ellipsoid is ellipsoidal height. National datums differ, so do not mix coordinates from different systems.

sections.heading: Map projections and UTM
sections.text: A map projection turns the curved Earth into a plane and distorts distance, area, shape or direction. UTM is a transverse Mercator system in 6° zones. Each zone has a central meridian with scale factor 0.9996 and a false easting of 500,000 m. Grid convergence is the angle between grid north and true north. Approximate it by γ ≈ Δλ sin φ, where Δλ is longitude difference from the central meridian. Example: φ = 6° N, Δλ = 1.5°. γ ≈ 1.5 × sin 6° = 1.5 × 0.10453 = 0.157°, about 9.4 arcminutes.

sections.heading: Datum transformations
sections.text: Changing from one datum to another needs transformation parameters, not a simple shift. The Helmert 7-parameter transformation uses three translations, three rotations and a scale change. Use the official parameters for the area. National datums, projections, height systems and transformation parameters differ. Check the national mapping agency or the current official source before using coordinates.

keyPoints: The geoid is a gravity equipotential surface approximating mean sea level; the ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical fit.
A horizontal datum fixes ellipsoid, origin and orientation; a vertical datum fixes the zero for heights.
UTM is transverse Mercator in 6° zones with central meridian scale factor 0.9996 and false easting 500,000 m.
Grid convergence is approximately γ ≈ Δλ sin φ, where Δλ is longitude difference from the central meridian.
Datum transformation needs official parameters; a simple coordinate shift is not enough.
National datums, projections and height systems differ, so check the national mapping agency.

en.title: Least-Squares Adjustment of Survey Observations
en.short: Observation and normal equations, residuals, covariance and error ellipses in survey adjustment.

sections.heading: Observation equations
sections.text: Least squares treats each measurement as an observation equation. For linearised problems, l + v = A x, where l is observed minus computed from approximate coordinates, v is the residual, A holds partial derivatives, and x is the correction to unknowns. Nonlinear distances and angles are linearised about approximate coordinates. Redundancy r = n − u, where n is observations and u unknowns. Redundancy allows residuals and quality estimates.

sections.heading: Normal equations
sections.text: Minimising Σv² gives normal equations AᵀA x = Aᵀl, so x = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀl. Adjusted unknowns are approximate values plus x. Example: two measurements of one height are 10.004 m and 9.996 m, with approximate height 10.000 m. Then l = [+0.004, −0.004] m, A = [1; 1]. AᵀA = 2, Aᵀl = 0, so x = 0. Adjusted height = 10.000 m. Residuals v = A x − l = [−0.004, +0.004] m. Check.

sections.heading: Residuals and covariance
sections.text: After adjustment, compute vᵀv. The reference variance is σ0² = vᵀv ÷ r. The covariance matrix of unknowns is Σx = σ0²(AᵀA)⁻¹. Its diagonal gives variances; off-diagonals give covariances. For a point, the 2×2 east-north block gives an error ellipse. Its semi-axes are c√λ1 and c√λ2, where λ1 and λ2 are eigenvalues and c is a chosen scale factor. The eigenvector of λ1 gives the major-axis direction. Here vᵀv = 0.000032 m², r = 2−1 = 1, so σ0² = 0.000032 m².

sections.heading: Networks and blunders
sections.text: In a traverse or network, unknowns are station coordinates. Distance and angle equations are linearised and solved together. Adjustment spreads small random errors according to geometry and weights; it does not remove gross errors. Blunder detection uses redundancy: inspect standardised residuals, v_i ÷ σ_vi, and apply statistical tests or data-snooping. A large residual may be a blunder or a poor weight. Remove or reweight suspect observations only after checking, then adjust again.

keyPoints: Observation equation: l + v = A x, with l observed minus computed, v residual and x correction.
Normal equations: AᵀA x = Aᵀl, so x = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀl.
Residuals are v = A x − l; adjusted values are approximate values plus x.
Reference variance is σ0² = vᵀv ÷ r, where r = n − u.
Covariance of unknowns is Σx = σ0²(AᵀA)⁻¹; its 2×2 point block gives the error ellipse.
Least squares adjusts random errors; blunder detection uses redundancy and standardised residuals.

en.title: Route Surveying: Horizontal and Vertical Curves
en.short: Route location, horizontal and vertical curves, setting-out data and simple earthworks.

sections.heading: Route location
sections.text:
Route surveying fixes the line of a road, railway or pipeline. It moves from desk study and reconnaissance to preliminary survey and final location. The surveyor maps the corridor, controls gradients and balances cut and fill. Design standards and permitted radii differ by country, so use the national road design manual.

The horizontal alignment is the plan; the vertical alignment is the profile. Tangent points are where a curve joins a straight.

sections.heading: Horizontal curves
sections.text:
A simple circular curve has radius R and turns through Δ. Tangent points PC and PT join the straights; the tangents meet at PI. Elements:
T = R tan(Δ/2); L = πRΔ/180; E = R(sec(Δ/2) − 1); M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2)); C = 2R sin(Δ/2).
Example: R = 300 m, Δ = 40°. T = 300 tan20° = 109.19 m; L = 300 × 40 × π ÷ 180 = 209.44 m.
A compound curve joins arcs of different radii curving the same way. A transition curve, often a clothoid, changes radius gradually, allowing superelevation (banking) to be introduced.

sections.heading: Vertical curves
sections.text:
A vertical curve joins gradients smoothly. BVC and EVC are its ends; VPI is the tangent intersection. With grades g1 and g2 in percent, length L and distance x from BVC:
y = yBVC + (g1/100)x + ((g2 − g1)x²) ÷ (200L).
The high or low point is at x = −g1L ÷ (g2 − g1).
Example: g1 = +2%, g2 = −3%, L = 200 m, yBVC = 100.000 m. At x = 80 m: y = 100 + 1.6 − 0.8 = 100.800 m.

sections.heading: Setting out and earthwork
sections.text:
Set out a curve by deflection angles. For arc length l from PC, δ = l ÷ (2R) radians, or δ° = 90l ÷ (πR). Example: l = 30 m, R = 300 m gives δ = 0.05 rad = 2.86°.
Earthwork by average end area: V = (A1 + A2) ÷ 2 × d. For trench, V = width × depth × length. Example: 0.8 m × 1.2 m × 150 m gives 144 m³.

keyPoints: Route surveying locates and sets out road, railway and pipeline alignments; design standards vary by country.
Simple circular curve: T = R tan(Δ/2); L = πRΔ/180; E = R(sec(Δ/2) − 1); M = R(1 − cos(Δ/2)); C = 2R sin(Δ/2).
A compound curve joins arcs of different radii curving the same way; a transition curve changes radius gradually.
Vertical curve: y = yBVC + (g1/100)x + ((g2 − g1)x²)/(200L), with grades in percent.
Deflection angle for setting out: δ = l/(2R) radians.
Average end area volume: V = (A1 + A2)/2 × d; trench volume = width × depth × length.

en.title: Engineering Surveying: Setting Out and Deformation Monitoring
en.short: Setting out from control, GNSS and total station stakeout, as-built checks and deformation monitoring.

sections.heading: Setting out from control
sections.text:
Setting out places a design point or line on the ground in the correct position and level. It starts from control: fixed stations with known coordinates and heights. The designer supplies coordinates, chainages, offsets or levels. The surveyor computes bearing and distance from control to each point, then marks it with a peg, nail or paint.

Buildings are set out from grid lines and corners, roads from the centreline and offsets, pipelines from alignment and invert levels (inside bottom of pipe), and structures from column or pile coordinates. Close back to control to catch errors early.

sections.heading: Instruments and checks
sections.text:
A total station measures angles and distance and computes coordinates. In stakeout mode it shows the turn and distance to a design point. A GNSS receiver in real-time kinematic (RTK) mode fixes position from satellites with corrections from a base station or network. RTK is fast in open sky but weaker under trees, beside tall buildings or where signals reflect. Check GNSS stakeout with a total station or independent control.

Record the station, backsight, point number and marks. Use the same datum and projection as the design; a mismatch shifts every point.

sections.heading: As-built and deformation
sections.text:
An as-built survey measures completed work and compares it with the design. It records positions, levels, dimensions and changes. Verticality checks test how far a column, wall or tower leans from plumb, using a total station, plumb laser or inclinometer (tilt sensor).

Deformation monitoring repeats observations over time to detect movement of a structure or the ground. Observations are made from stable reference points outside the zone to prisms (reflecting targets) fixed on the structure. Changes larger than measurement noise are investigated. Frequency and alarm levels come from the design.

sections.heading: Accuracy and example
sections.text:
Accuracy depends on the work and national code. Earthworks may allow centimetres, structural steel millimetres, and deformation work finer.

Example: A (1000.000, 1000.000) m, P (1012.000, 1016.000) m. ΔE = 12.000 m, ΔN = 16.000 m. Distance = √(12² + 16²) = 20.000 m. Bearing clockwise from north = arctan(12 ÷ 16) = 36°52′12″.

keyPoints: Setting out converts design coordinates into bearing and distance from control, then marks the point.
Distance = √(ΔE² + ΔN²); bearing clockwise from north = arctan(ΔE ÷ ΔN), adjusted to the correct quadrant.
Total stations suit precise stakeout; GNSS RTK is fast in open sky but needs checking near obstructions.
As-built surveys compare completed work with design; verticality checks test lean from plumb.
Deformation monitoring repeats observations from stable reference points and investigates changes above noise.
Tolerances vary by work, project and country; check the specification and current national code.

en.title: Cadastral Surveying and Land Registration
en.short: Parcels, boundary surveys, cadastral maps, land registration and the surveyor’s legal role, with a Nigerian example.

sections.heading: Parcels and boundaries
sections.text: A parcel is a defined area of land with boundaries and usually a unique number in a cadastral system. A boundary survey finds where those boundaries lie on the ground. The surveyor ties the parcel to control points, measures sides and angles, and places or checks boundary marks called beacons. The result is a survey plan recording the parcel’s geometry. Boundaries may be fixed by coordinates, physical features, or both; practice differs by country.

sections.heading: Cadastral maps
sections.text: A cadastral map shows parcels, their boundaries, identifiers and often the land rights attached to them. It is built from cadastral surveys and updated as parcels are subdivided or merged. A cadastre is the wider record: the map plus the register of parcels and rights. Cadastral maps support taxation, planning, land markets and dispute resolution. They differ from topographic maps, which show terrain and features rather than legal parcels.

sections.heading: Land registration
sections.text: Land registration is the official recording of rights and interests in land, usually at a land registry. In deeds registration, documents are recorded. In title registration, the state registers the title itself and may guarantee it, as in the Torrens system. Laws and procedures differ by country. In Nigeria, land is governed mainly by the Land Use Act 1978, and state governors grant statutory rights of occupancy. A Certificate of Occupancy is evidence of a granted right, but not every parcel has one. Practice varies between states.

sections.heading: Surveyor’s role
sections.text: The surveyor’s legal role is to provide reliable boundary and parcel evidence, not to decide who owns land. A registered surveyor signs and seals plans used in registration and court cases. In Nigeria, surveyors are regulated by the Surveyors Council of Nigeria (SURCON). A made-up case: in Lagos State, a seller and buyer use a registered surveyor to survey a plot and tie it to control. The plan and beacons help the state land registry record the transaction. If a neighbour claims an overlap, the court decides ownership, using survey evidence.

keyPoints: A parcel is a defined land area with boundaries and usually a unique cadastral identifier.
A boundary survey fixes or checks parcel boundaries on the ground and produces a survey plan.
A cadastral map shows parcels and boundaries; a cadastre adds the register of rights.
Land registration records rights in land, by deeds or by title; laws and procedures differ by country.
In Nigeria, the Land Use Act 1978 and state land registries shape registration, and SURCON regulates surveyors.
A surveyor provides boundary evidence but does not decide ownership; courts decide disputes and registries record rights.

en.title: Photogrammetry and UAV Mapping
en.short: Measuring from aerial and UAV images: camera geometry, stereo, orientation, DEMs and orthophotos.

sections.heading: Images and camera geometry
sections.text: Photogrammetry measures objects from photographs. Aerial photography is taken from aircraft; UAV mapping uses small drones. Vertical photos look straight down and are usual for mapping; oblique photos show building sides. Overlap is needed for stereo and image matching. Camera geometry has interior orientation (focal length, principal point, lens distortion) and exterior orientation (camera position and attitude). The principal point is near the image centre, and attitude means how the camera is tilted. For a vertical photo, scale S = f ÷ H, where f is focal length and H is flying height above the ground, in the same unit. Example: f = 20 mm and H = 200 m = 200,000 mm give S = 20 ÷ 200,000 = 1:10,000. A 10 mm image distance represents 100 m on the ground. Ground sample distance is the ground size of one pixel: GSD = pixel size × H ÷ f; with 0.005 mm pixels, GSD = 0.005 × 200,000 ÷ 20 = 50 mm.

sections.heading: Stereo and orientation
sections.text: Stereoscopy is viewing two overlapping photos so the ground appears in 3D. Parallax is the shift of the same point between the two images; points at different heights have different parallax, which allows height measurement. Relative orientation fixes the photos to each other; absolute orientation fits the stereo model to ground coordinates using ground control points (GCPs), points whose coordinates are known. Modern software also uses bundle adjustment, which jointly refines camera positions, orientations and object points. Good GCP spread and camera calibration control accuracy.

sections.heading: Products, limits and uses
sections.text: Image matching produces a point cloud, then a digital elevation model (DEM), a grid of ground or surface heights. An orthophoto is an image corrected for tilt and height shift so it has map scale. Accuracy depends on GSD, overlap, texture (image detail), GCPs and processing. Check accuracy against independent checkpoints (known points not used in processing). Flight rules and mapping standards vary by country; in Nigeria, UAV operations are regulated by the Nigerian Civil Aviation Authority. Limitations include wind, short endurance, small payload, vegetation, water, shadows and legal privacy or airspace limits. Uses include topographic mapping, construction progress, mining volumes, agriculture and disaster assessment.

keyPoints: Photogrammetry measures objects from overlapping photographs; UAV mapping uses small drones.
For a vertical photo, scale S = f ÷ H and ground sample distance GSD = pixel size × H ÷ f.
Parallax is the image shift of a point between overlapping photos and it reveals height.
Relative orientation links photos; absolute orientation uses ground control points to fit them to ground coordinates.
A DEM stores heights and an orthophoto is corrected for tilt and height shift so it has map scale.
Accuracy depends on GSD, overlap, camera calibration, GCPs and independent checkpoints, and UAV rules vary by country.

en.title: Remote Sensing
en.short: The electromagnetic spectrum, platforms and sensors, resolutions, image interpretation, indices and classification.

sections.heading: Spectrum and platforms
sections.text: Remote sensing measures reflected or emitted energy from a distance. The electromagnetic spectrum runs from short gamma and X-rays through ultraviolet, visible light, near-infrared (NIR), shortwave infrared, thermal infrared and microwaves. Most optical sensors use reflected sunlight; thermal sensors record emitted heat; radar uses microwaves and is active, sending its own pulse. A platform carries the sensor: satellite, aircraft, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) or ground mast. Passive sensors record natural radiation. Active sensors supply energy and measure the return.

sections.heading: Four resolutions
sections.text: Four resolutions describe an image. Spatial resolution is the ground size of one pixel; a 10 m sensor gives 10 m × 10 m = 100 m² per pixel. Spectral resolution is the number and width of wavelength bands; many narrow bands allow finer material discrimination. Radiometric resolution is the number of brightness levels, often stored as bits; 8 bits give 256 levels. Temporal resolution is the revisit interval, the time between repeated images of the same place.

sections.heading: Interpreting images
sections.text: Image interpretation reads tone or colour, texture, pattern, shape, size, shadow and context. A dark tone may mean water or wet soil; a bright red tone on a false-colour infrared image often marks healthy vegetation. Analysts combine field visits with images, because one clue alone can mislead. A small case: a planner maps a new settlement by noting rectangular roofs, straight roads and bare soil, then checks boundaries on the ground.

sections.heading: Indices and classification
sections.text: Simple indices compare bands. The normalised difference vegetation index (NDVI) is (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red), from −1 to +1. With NIR = 0.50 and red = 0.10: (0.50 − 0.10) ÷ (0.50 + 0.10) = 0.40 ÷ 0.60 = 0.67, suggesting green vegetation. Classification assigns pixels to land-cover classes such as water, forest, cropland and built-up land. Supervised classification uses labelled training samples; unsupervised classification groups pixels by spectral similarity. Accuracy is checked against known points, often with a confusion matrix. Applications include crop monitoring, land-use change and erosion or flood mapping.

keyPoints: Remote sensing records reflected or emitted energy from a distance.
Passive sensors record natural radiation; active sensors emit energy and measure the return.
Spatial resolution is pixel ground size; a 10 m pixel covers 100 m².
Spectral resolution is number and width of bands; radiometric is brightness levels; temporal is revisit interval.
NDVI = (NIR − Red) ÷ (NIR + Red).
Supervised classification uses labelled training samples; unsupervised groups by spectral similarity.

en.title: Cartography and Map Production
en.short: Map design, scale, generalization, symbols, colour, layout and producing checked topographic and thematic maps.

sections.heading: Purpose and scale
sections.text: Cartography is the art and science of making maps. A map is a selected, simplified and symbolised model of space, made for a stated purpose and audience. Before drawing, decide the purpose, the area, the scale and the projection. Scale is the ratio of map distance to ground distance. At 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map represents 50,000 cm, or 500 m, on the ground. A 2 cm feature is therefore 1 km long. A 20 m building would be 20 ÷ 50,000 = 0.0004 m, or 0.4 mm, on the map: too small to draw to scale.

sections.heading: Generalization and symbols
sections.text: Generalization is the controlled simplification of detail to suit the scale and purpose. It includes selection, simplification, smoothing, aggregation, displacement and classification. At small scales, many features cannot be shown; a town may become a point symbol and a winding river a smoother line. Symbolization turns data into marks: point symbols for wells or schools, line symbols for roads and rivers, area fills for land use. Symbols should be clear, distinguishable and matched to the data type. Labels must not overlap and should follow the feature where possible.

sections.heading: Colour, layout and production
sections.text: Colour carries meaning. Use hue, value and saturation deliberately. Sequential schemes suit ordered data such as rainfall; diverging schemes suit data around a middle value; qualitative hues suit categories such as soil types. Check legibility in greyscale and for colour blindness. Layout arranges title, legend, scale bar, north arrow, source, date, inset and neatline so the map reads in a clear order. Production is a workflow: capture and edit survey or GIS data, generalise, symbolise, label, lay out, then check topology, attributes, positional accuracy, currency and legibility against the stated purpose. Topographic maps show relief, drainage, transport, settlement and land cover; thematic maps emphasise one theme, such as land use or population. Follow the relevant national mapping standard and record metadata.

keyPoints: A map is a selected, simplified and symbolised model of space made for a stated purpose and audience.
Scale is map distance ÷ ground distance; at 1:50,000, 1 cm represents 500 m on the ground.
Generalization includes selection, simplification, smoothing, aggregation, displacement and classification.
Use point, line and area symbols that match the data and do not overlap labels.
Colour schemes should match data: sequential for order, diverging for a middle value, qualitative for categories.
Production ends with quality checks on topology, attributes, accuracy, currency and legibility before export or print.

en.title: GIS Spatial Data Models and Basic Analysis
en.short: Vector and raster models, topology, attributes, georeferencing, editing, and basic overlay, query and buffer analysis.

sections.heading: Vector and raster
sections.text: Vector and raster are the two main spatial data models. Vector stores points, lines and polygons as coordinates, so it suits discrete objects such as roads or parcels. Raster stores a grid of cells, each with a value, so it suits continuous surfaces such as elevation and thematic maps such as land cover. Cell size is the spatial resolution. Topology describes spatial relationships: adjacency, connectivity and containment. Vector topology is stored explicitly and checked by rules; raster topology is implicit in neighbouring cells. Attributes are non-spatial values in a table, linked by an identifier or cell value.

sections.heading: Georeferencing and data
sections.text: Georeferencing assigns coordinates in a known coordinate reference system, which is defined by a datum and, for projected systems, a map projection. Without correct georeferencing, layers will not align. Data input includes digitising, scanning, GNSS, remote sensing and existing databases. Editing corrects geometry and attributes and enforces topology rules. Accuracy includes positional accuracy, attribute accuracy and logical consistency. Check datum, projection and scale first.

sections.heading: Basic analysis
sections.text: An attribute query selects features by table values, for example wards with population above 50,000. A spatial query selects by location, such as parcels within 1 km of a road. A buffer creates a polygon at a set distance around a feature. Overlay combines layers: vector overlay uses intersection or union; raster overlay uses map algebra cell by cell. In a made-up Kano, Nigeria planning case, clinics are points and wards are polygons. A 500 m buffer around the clinics shows wards within that straight-line distance. A 30 m raster cell covers 30 × 30 = 900 m²; a 10 m cell covers 100 m², so the finer grid has nine times as many cells over the same area.

sections.heading: Model choice
sections.text: Model choice changes analysis and accuracy. Vector is strong for precise boundaries and networks, but overlay can create slivers (thin unwanted polygons) and needs clean topology. Raster is strong for continuous data and map algebra, but cell size limits detail and mixed cells blur boundaries. Source scale and positional accuracy matter most. Choose the model that matches the question.

keyPoints: Vector stores points, lines and polygons; raster stores grid cells with values.
Topology records adjacency, connectivity and containment; vector topology is explicit, raster topology is implicit.
Georeferencing places data in a known coordinate reference system; a wrong datum or projection stops layers aligning.
Attribute queries select by table values; spatial queries select by location; buffers create zones at a set distance.
Vector overlay uses intersection or union; raster overlay uses map algebra cell by cell.
Raster accuracy depends on cell size: cell area = cell size², and mixed cells blur boundaries.

en.title: Spatial Databases and Spatial Data Infrastructure
en.short: Database concepts, spatial SQL, indexing, metadata, data quality and SDI for sharing geospatial data.

sections.heading: Databases and SQL
sections.text: A database is an organised collection of data. A database management system (DBMS) stores, retrieves and protects it. In a relational database, data sit in tables of rows (records) and columns (fields). A primary key uniquely identifies a row; a foreign key links to a row in another table. SQL (Structured Query Language) defines and queries these tables: SELECT chooses columns and rows, and JOIN combines tables on a shared key.

sections.heading: Spatial databases and indexing
sections.text: A spatial database adds geometry types (point, line, polygon) and spatial functions to a database. B-tree indexes suit numbers and text; spatial indexes such as the R-tree group nearby objects so a search need not scan every row. PostGIS adds spatial types and functions to PostgreSQL. A query: SELECT parcel_id FROM parcels WHERE ST_Intersects(geom, ST_Buffer(road_geom, 10)); finds parcels within 10 map units of a road.

sections.heading: Metadata and quality
sections.text: Metadata is data about data: source, date, coordinate reference system, owner, accuracy and licence. ISO 19115 is an international standard for geographic metadata. Data quality includes completeness, positional accuracy, attribute accuracy, logical consistency, temporal quality and lineage (the history of the data). Standards make sharing possible. The Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) publishes open standards such as Simple Features for geometry and Web Map Service (WMS) and Web Feature Service (WFS) for serving maps and features over the web.

sections.heading: Spatial data infrastructure
sections.text: A spatial data infrastructure (SDI) is the policies, standards, technology, people and data that let organisations find, access and use geospatial data. It includes catalogues, metadata, web services and sharing rules. An SDI aims to avoid duplicate datasets and conflicting boundaries. For example, a city planning office and a water utility both need roads. If the survey department publishes one authoritative road dataset with metadata and OGC services, both use the same version. The European Union’s INSPIRE directive is one regional example; national SDIs differ, so check local policy.

keyPoints: A relational database stores data in tables; a primary key identifies each row and a foreign key links tables.
SQL defines and queries relational data; SELECT chooses columns and rows, and JOIN combines tables.
Spatial databases add geometry types and functions; spatial indexes such as R-trees avoid scanning every row.
Metadata records source, date, coordinate reference system, accuracy and licence; ISO 19115 is a geographic metadata standard.
Data quality includes completeness, positional and attribute accuracy, logical consistency, temporal quality and lineage.
An SDI combines policy, standards, technology, people and data so organisations share authoritative geospatial data; national arrangements differ, so check local policy.

en.title: Hydrographic Surveying: Sounding, Tides and Charts
en.short: Bathymetric sounding, tide and datum reduction, positioning, sonar and chart production.

sections.heading: Sounding on water
sections.text: Hydrographic surveying measures depths and features in rivers, lakes, harbours and seas so that safe charts can be made. A bathymetric sounding is one depth measurement. An echo sounder sends a sound pulse down and times its return; depth = c × t ÷ 2, where c is the speed of sound in water, about 1500 m/s but changing with temperature, salinity and pressure. Multibeam sonar measures a swath of depths, while side-scan sonar images the seabed texture. The survey platform moves, so each sounding needs a position and a time.

sections.heading: Tide and datum
sections.text: Depths must refer to a chart datum, a fixed low-water level chosen by the national hydrographic authority. It is often Lowest Astronomical Tide, but this varies by country. A tide gauge records the water level. Reduced depth = measured depth + transducer draft − tide height above datum. Example: measured depth 12.40 m, transducer draft 0.50 m, tide 1.80 m. Reduced depth = 12.40 + 0.50 − 1.80 = 11.10 m. If the tide is below datum, its height is negative.

sections.heading: Positioning and charts
sections.text: Each sounding is positioned by GNSS, by intersection from shore stations, or by acoustic positioning from a vessel. Horizontal and vertical control must be checked. Soundings are corrected for tide, draft, sound speed and vessel motion, then plotted with depth contours, hazards, aids to navigation and notes. The International Hydrographic Organization (IHO) publishes standards, but national authorities issue charts and set limits. Accuracy depends on position, depth, tide and calibration; independent check lines help.

sections.heading: Safety and limits
sections.text: Work on water adds risks: drowning, weather, currents, traffic and equipment failure. Use a suitable vessel, life jackets, radio, weather forecasts and permits. Survey accuracy is limited by moving platforms, sound reflection, poor satellite view and tide errors. Record metadata and check the final chart against the survey specification.

keyPoints: Hydrographic surveying measures depths and seabed features to produce safe navigation charts.
Echo sounder depth = c × t ÷ 2, with c the speed of sound in water.
Reduced depth = measured depth + transducer draft − tide height above chart datum.
Chart datum is a low-water reference set nationally, often but not always Lowest Astronomical Tide.
Soundings need accurate position, time, tide and calibration, checked with independent lines.
Water work requires vessel safety, weather planning, life jackets and permits.

en.title: Professional Practice, Ethics and Registration in Surveying
en.short: Ethics, registration, contracts, liability, safety and quality assurance for surveyors.

sections.heading: Ethics and conduct
sections.text:
Professional ethics are the standards of honesty, competence and fairness expected of a surveyor. The surveyor owes duties to the public, the client and the profession. A conflict of interest must be disclosed, and confidential client information must be protected.

Case: Ngozi, a surveyor in Enugu, is asked to move a boundary line on a plan to favour a client. Ethical practice means refusing, recording the true measurement and explaining the legal position. A surveyor must work only within their competence.

sections.heading: Registration and regulation
sections.text: Registration is the official listing that gives a person the legal right to practise and use a protected title. Regulation is the system of rules and discipline that keeps standards. In Nigeria, the Surveyors Council of Nigeria (SURCON) registers and regulates surveyors, while the Nigerian Institution of Surveyors (NIS) is the professional body. Registration rules, titles and renewal requirements differ by country, so check the current authority. Many authorities also require continuing professional development (CPD).

sections.heading: Contracts and liability
sections.text: A contract is a legally binding agreement. A surveying contract should state the scope, deliverables, fees, time, responsibilities and any limits of liability. Liability means legal responsibility for loss or damage. A surveyor may be liable for negligence, which is failure to use reasonable care and skill. Professional indemnity insurance covers claims, but it does not replace good practice. Some contracts try to limit liability, but whether such clauses are enforceable varies by country.

sections.heading: Safety and quality
sections.text:
Safety in surveying means managing risks in the field: traffic, construction sites, weather, water and lone working. A risk assessment identifies hazards and controls before work starts. Quality assurance (QA) is the planned system that prevents errors, through calibrated instruments, standard procedures, independent checks and records. Quality control checks the finished work.

Example: before setting out a building, two surveyors independently check the control coordinates and the instrument level. The check is recorded.

keyPoints: Professional ethics require honesty, competence and public safety before a client’s wishes.
Registration is a legal licence to practise; in Nigeria SURCON registers surveyors and NIS is the professional institution.
Registration rules and protected titles differ by country, so check the current authority.
A clear contract should state scope, deliverables, fees, time and limits of liability.
Surveyors can be liable for negligence, and professional indemnity insurance protects against claims.
Risk assessments and documented quality assurance reduce field and office errors.

en.title: Advanced Geodesy and Earth Deformation
en.short: Gravity, geoid, reference frames, Earth tides and GNSS monitoring of crustal deformation.

sections.heading: Gravity and geoid
sections.text: The gravity field is the gravitational attraction plus centrifugal effect of Earth’s rotation. Its potential is usually expanded in spherical harmonics. The geoid is the equipotential surface that best fits mean sea level; heights above it are orthometric heights. Geoid modelling combines gravity measurements, satellite gravity missions and a reference ellipsoid. A gravity anomaly is the difference between observed gravity and a reference value at the same point. The geoid is not the ellipsoid: it undulates by roughly −100 m to +80 m worldwide, so a local model is needed for accurate heights.

sections.heading: Frames and tides
sections.text: A reference frame is the realised set of stations and coordinates used to express positions; the International Terrestrial Reference Frame (ITRF) is a widely used global frame. WGS 84 is the frame used by GPS. Earth tides are periodic deformations of the solid Earth caused mainly by the Moon and Sun. They move the ground vertically by up to a few tens of centimetres. The same tidal forces also raise ocean tides, and the shifting ocean load deforms the crust as well. Tidal corrections are therefore applied in precise positioning.

sections.heading: GNSS deformation
