sections.text: GNSS receivers measure ranges to satellites and compute positions. Repeated or continuous observations give station coordinates and velocities. A network across a fault or volcano can show slow strain accumulation, coseismic jumps and postseismic relaxation. InSAR, VLBI, SLR and DORIS provide complementary crustal deformation and frame information. Example: a 20 km baseline extends by 40 mm in 5 years. Strain = 40 mm ÷ 20,000,000 mm = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶, or 2 microstrain. Rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 5 = 4.0 × 10⁻⁷ per year.

sections.heading: Model limits
sections.text: A static model assumes steady velocity or a rigid block, so it cannot represent earthquakes, seasonal loading or slow changes in strain rate. A kinematic model allows time-varying motion but needs dense, clean data and assumptions about noise and discontinuities. Both depend on the reference frame, monument stability, atmospheric delays and tidal models. Results are therefore estimates with uncertainty, not exact truth.

keyPoints: The geoid is an equipotential surface of Earth’s gravity field, not the reference ellipsoid.
A reference frame is a realised set of stations and coordinates; ITRF is a global example and WGS 84 is used by GPS.
Earth tides are periodic solid-Earth deformations caused mainly by the Moon and Sun and must be corrected in precise work.
GNSS gives positions and velocities that reveal strain accumulation, coseismic jumps and postseismic motion.
Strain = change in baseline length ÷ original baseline length; strain rate = strain ÷ time.
Static models assume steady or rigid motion, while kinematic models allow time variation but need dense reliable data.

en.title: Advanced Adjustment and Estimation Theory
en.short: Robust estimation, variance components, datum defects, Kalman filtering and large-network adjustment.

sections.heading: Least squares and validation
sections.text: Least squares assumes errors have zero mean, known covariance and a linearised model. It minimises v^T W v, where v is the residual vector and W the weight matrix. The estimate is x_hat = (A^T W A)^−1 A^T W l. The unit variance is σ0² = v^T W v ÷ (n − u), with n observations and u unknowns. Parameter covariance is Qx = σ0² (A^T W A)^−1. Validation checks residuals, the chi-square test and the stochastic model. Reliability is the network’s ability to detect blunders (internal) and to limit their effect on results (external).

sections.heading: Robust estimation and variance components
sections.text: Outliers break least squares. Robust estimation uses M-estimators, which limit the influence of large residuals; Huber’s estimator is quadratic near zero and linear beyond a tuning constant. Variance component estimation finds unknown variance factors for groups of observations, often by Helmert’s method, then reweights and iterates. Example: two equal-weight observations of one height, 10.002 m and 10.006 m, give x = 10.004 m. Residuals are +0.002 m and −0.002 m. v^T v = 8×10^−6 m², so with n − u = 1, σ0² = 8×10^−6 m² and σ0 = 0.0028 m.

sections.heading: Datum defects and large networks
sections.text: A datum defect is a rank deficiency: the observations cannot fix origin, orientation or scale. Free network adjustment applies minimum or inner constraints; the covariance matrix is then singular or constrained. Large networks exploit sparsity in the normal matrix, using block elimination or iterative solvers, and avoid forming the full inverse.

sections.heading: Kalman filtering
sections.text: Kalman filtering is recursive least squares for dynamic systems. Prediction: x_minus = F x + B u and P_minus = F P F^T + Q. Update: K = P_minus H^T (H P_minus H^T + R)^−1, x = x_minus + K(z − H x_minus), P = (I − K H) P_minus. It assumes a linear model and known Gaussian process and measurement noise. Model validation remains essential.

keyPoints: Least-squares solution: x_hat = (A^T W A)^−1 A^T W l.
Unit variance: σ0² = v^T W v ÷ (n − u); parameter covariance: Qx = σ0² (A^T W A)^−1.
Least squares assumes zero-mean errors, a correct weight matrix and a linearised model.
Robust M-estimators limit outliers; variance component estimation estimates unknown group variances.
Datum defects need constraints or free-network methods; large networks use sparse matrix techniques.
Kalman gain: K = P_minus H^T (H P_minus H^T + R)^−1, with prediction and update steps.

en.title: Advanced Spatial Analysis and Geostatistics
en.short: Spatial statistics, variograms, kriging, networks, 3D and 4D models, and uncertainty in prediction.

sections.heading: Spatial statistics and variograms
sections.text:
Spatial statistics treats a mapped variable as a random field: nearby values tend to be alike (spatial autocorrelation). For lag h (the separation distance between point pairs), the experimental semivariance is γ(h) = 1 ÷ (2N(h)) Σ [z(xi) − z(xi+h)]², where N(h) is the number of pairs. A fitted variogram model gives nugget, sill and range. The nugget is small-scale variation and measurement error, the sill is the plateau, and the range is where correlation becomes weak.

Example: values 10, 12, 11 and 15 at x = 0, 1, 2 and 3. For h = 1 the squared differences are 4, 1 and 16, so γ(1) = (4 + 1 + 16) ÷ (2 × 3) = 3.5.

sections.heading: Kriging and interpolation
sections.text: Kriging is a family of weighted interpolators. Ordinary kriging predicts at an unsampled point from a fitted variogram and is best linear unbiased under its assumptions. Its weights solve a linear system with the variogram and sum to one. It also returns a kriging variance, a local uncertainty measure. Simpler methods include inverse distance weighting, splines and nearest neighbour; they do not model spatial covariance similarly. Cross-validation tests the model by leaving points out and predicting them.

sections.heading: Networks and 3D models
sections.text: Network analysis works on connected lines, not open space. It finds shortest paths, service areas and optimal facility locations, supporting road, water and emergency planning. Three-dimensional models represent terrain, buildings and subsurface layers with triangulated irregular networks (TINs), voxels (3D pixels) or building information models (BIM). Four-dimensional models add time, for example settlement, flooding or construction progress. They help infrastructure siting, land-use and environmental decisions.

sections.heading: Uncertainty and decisions
sections.text: Uncertainty in spatial prediction comes from sparse samples, measurement error, model choice and scale. Report prediction variance, validate with independent data and use Monte Carlo simulation (repeated random trials) to propagate error into decisions. A flood map, a contaminated-site estimate or a route plan should state its confidence and limits. Codes for spatial data and survey practice differ by country; check the national source.

keyPoints: Experimental semivariance: γ(h) = 1 ÷ (2N(h)) Σ [z(xi) − z(xi+h)]².
A variogram model is described by nugget, sill and range.
Ordinary kriging weights solve Σ λj γ(xi,xj) + μ = γ(xi,x0) with Σ λj = 1.
Kriging is best linear unbiased under its model assumptions and gives a kriging variance.
Network analysis finds shortest paths, service areas and location-allocation on connected networks.
3D models represent volume; 4D adds time; report and validate uncertainty before decisions.

en.title: Research Methods in Geoinformatics
en.short: Dissertation design, sampling, geospatial data collection, analysis, ethics and reproducibility.

sections.heading: Design and questions
sections.text: A dissertation is a small, bounded study that answers a clear question. Start with a research question, not a topic: it names the population, the place, the variables and the expected relationship. A literature review is not a list of summaries. It shows what is known, where studies disagree and which gap your question addresses. The design follows from the question: field survey, secondary GIS analysis, remote sensing, case study or mixed methods. Record the unit of analysis (the thing studied), the study area and the time period.

sections.heading: Sampling and data
sections.text: Sampling selects cases from a sampling frame (the list of all units in the population). Probability sampling gives every unit a known chance and supports generalisation; non-probability sampling is common in fieldwork but limits inference. Spatial sampling must cover the area, not just convenient roads. Data may come from GNSS, total stations, imagery, existing layers, questionnaires or interviews. For each source, state positional accuracy, attribute accuracy, completeness and date. Secondary data may lack lineage (source history).

sections.heading: Analysis and limits
sections.text: Choose analysis that matches the question and data: maps, overlay, buffers, spatial statistics or regression. Do not treat a GIS overlay as proof of cause. Evidence has limits. GNSS may be poor under canopy; imagery may be cloud-covered; questionnaires record reported behaviour; old maps may be out of date. A validation sample checks interpretation. Example: if 200 buildings are mapped and 40 of them are visited to check the mapping, the validation sample is 40 ÷ 200 = 20%.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Seek ethics approval where your institution requires it. Obtain informed consent, protect personal data and consider location privacy, because coordinates can identify people or sensitive sites. Data protection law differs by country, so check the current local rule. A data management plan names files, metadata (data about the data), backups, access and retention. Reproducibility means another researcher can follow your methods and get the same result from the same data. Write plainly: state aim, methods, results and limitations, and cite sources fully.

keyPoints: A research question names the population, place, variables and expected relationship.
A literature review identifies the gap your question addresses, not just summaries.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling limits it.
Geospatial evidence is limited by positional accuracy, date, coverage and method.
Reproducibility requires documented data, metadata, software and methods.
Ethics approval, informed consent, location privacy and local data law apply.
